claim: Natural transformation is a major mode of horizontal gene transfer by which bacteria take up DNA directly from their environment.
source: Natural transformation is a major mode of horizontal gene transfer (Blokesch, 2017; Mell and Redfield, 2014), by which bacteria take up DNA directly from their environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blokesch, 2017 and Mell and Redfield, 2014.

claim: Through natural transformation, bacteria gain novel genetic information including metabolic traits, pathogenicity determinants and resistance genes.
source: In this way, bacteria gain novel genetic information, for example metabolic traits, pathogenicity determinants and resistance genes as a driving force for bacterial adaptation and evolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about horizontal gene transfer.

claim: Natural transformation enables pathogenic bacteria to adapt to the human host, making it clinically relevant.
source: By enabling pathogenic bacteria to adapt to the human host, natural transformation is clinically relevant.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the role of natural transformation in bacterial adaptation.

claim: Natural transformation is mediated by multi-component transport machineries consisting of competence proteins that are highly conserved throughout the bacterial world.
source: Natural transformation is a complex process mediated by multi-component transport machineries consisting of so-called competence proteins, which are highly conserved throughout the bacterial world (Averhoff, 2009; Chen et al., 2005; Koomey, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Averhoff, 2009; Chen et al., 2005; and Koomey, 1998.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, the natural transformation machinery spans the entire periplasm and connects the inner and outer membranes.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria this machinery spans the entire periplasm and connects the inner (IM) and outer membranes (OM), mediating DNA binding on the cell surface and subsequent translocation through the periplasm into the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about bacterial transformation machinery.

claim: Many conserved proteins of bacterial DNA uptake machineries are similar to components of protein secretion and type IV pilus biogenesis systems and often play a dual role.
source: Many conserved proteins of the bacterial DNA uptake machineries are similar to components of protein secretion and type IV pilus biogenesis systems and often play a dual role (Hobbs and Mattick, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hobbs and Mattick, 1993.

claim: Secretin proteins are conserved key components of natural transformation systems in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Members of the secretin protein family are conserved key components of natural transformation systems in Gram-negative bacteria, and also play important roles in protein secretion, type IV pilus extrusion and the assembly and extrusion of filamentous bacteriophages (Ayers et al., 2010; Korotkov et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ayers et al., 2010 and Korotkov et al., 2011.

claim: The OM-embedded C-terminal secretin domain likely provides an aperture for DNA and protein translocation through the outer membrane.
source: The OM-embedded C-terminal secretin domain likely provides an aperture for DNA and protein translocation through the OM, connecting the periplasm to the extracellular environment.
evidence: The claim involves speculative reasoning about the function of the secretin domain.

claim: Members of the secretin family form homo-oligomers consisting of 12 to 19 subunits surrounding a central channel.
source: The members of the secretin family form homo-oligomers consisting of 12 to 19 subunits surrounding a central channel (Bayan et al., 2006; Costa et al., 2015; Jain et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bayan et al., 2006; Costa et al., 2015; and Jain et al., 2011.

claim: The size of the secretin complex, its oligomeric state and the structures of its periplasmic N-terminal domains vary considerably between organisms.
source: The size of the complex, its oligomeric state and the structures of its periplasmic N-terminal domains vary considerably between organisms.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about secretin diversity.

claim: Koo et al. showed the overall structure of the secretin domain of PilQ from Pseudomonas aeruginosa at intermediate resolution.
source: Koo et al. (Koo et al., 2016) showed the overall structure of the secretin domain of PilQ from Pseudomonas aeruginosa at intermediate resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Koo et al., 2016.

claim: Atomic models from cryo-EM structures of type 2 and type 3 secretion systems revealed the conserved architecture of the secretin domain as a double β-barrel structure.
source: Moreover, atomic models from cryo-EM structures of type 2 (T2SS) (Yan et al., 2017) and type 3 (T3SS) secretion systems (Worrall et al., 2016) revealed the conserved architecture of the secretin domain as a double β-barrel ('barrel-in-barrel' structure) forming the inner gate and the external scaffold.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yan et al., 2017 and Worrall et al., 2016.

claim: The N-terminal domains of secretins consist of copies of stacked rings which form a periplasmic channel that connects to IM-associated proteins.
source: The N-terminal domains of secretins consist of copies of stacked rings which form a periplasmic channel that connects to IM-associated proteins, forming a multi-component secretion system.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about secretin structure.

claim: Structural information on the N domains of secretins is scarce, and the N0 domain is usually missing or disordered.
source: Structural information on the N domains is scarce, and the N0 domain is usually missing or disordered (Berry et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2016; Worrall et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2016; Worrall et al., 2016; and Yan et al., 2017.

claim: A unique secretin (PilQ) complex in Thermus thermophilus is essential for natural transformation and extrusion of type IV pili.
source: In previous studies we discovered a unique secretin (PilQ) complex in the thermophilic bacterium Thermus thermophilus, which is essential for natural transformation and extrusion of type IV pili (Friedrich et al., 2002; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Friedrich et al., 2002 and Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: T. thermophilus PilQ contains a thermostable C-terminal secretin domain and an exceptionally long N-terminal tail of six stacked rings (N0-N5).
source: We showed that T. thermophilus PilQ contains a thermostable C-terminal secretin domain and an exceptionally long N-terminal tail of six stacked rings (N0-N5) (Burkhardt et al., 2011; 2012; Salzer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2011; 2012; and Salzer et al., 2016.

claim: The in situ structure of the entire T4PS machinery determined by cryo-electron tomography revealed conformational changes of the N-terminal ring-forming domains in piliated and unpiliated states.
source: Furthermore, we determined the in situ structure of the entire T4PS machinery by cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) in the piliated and unpiliated state, revealing conformational changes of the N-terminal ring-forming domains (Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gold et al., 2015.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the 13-fold symmetric PilQ complex was determined at 7 Å resolution.
source: We now report a 7 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the 13-fold symmetric PilQ complex revealing unique molecular architecture.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A novel image processing tool, REcenter Particles (REP), was used to determine the structure of the large and flexible PilQ complex.
source: We used a novel image processing tool, REcenter Particles (REP), and state-of-the-art remote homology detection and modeling methods to determine the structure of the large and flexible PilQ complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: A crown-like density outside the outer membrane was found not to be part of PilQ.
source: A crown-like structure outside the outer membrane capping the secretin was found not to be part of PilQ.
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in the secretin domain disrupted the crown and abolished DNA uptake.
source: Mutations in the secretin domain disrupted the crown and abolished DNA uptake, suggesting a central role of the crown in natural transformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies.

claim: The crown plays a central role in natural transformation.
source: Mutations in the secretin domain disrupted the crown and abolished DNA uptake, suggesting a central role of the crown in natural transformation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Carbon-back-coated holey carbon films were used for cryo-EM sample preparation to ensure an even distribution of PilQ particles.
source: We used carbon-back-coated holey carbon films for cryo-EM sample preparation (Koo et al., 2016; Low et al., 2014; Reichow et al., 2010; Schraidt and Marlovits, 2011; Tosi et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2017) to ensure an even distribution of PilQ particles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple methodological papers.

claim: A large majority of the particle images are side views.
source: By this procedure, a large majority of the particle images are side views (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the micrograph shown in Figure 1.

claim: Top views were too rare to determine the stoichiometry of the complex reliably by two-dimensional classification.
source: Top views were too rare to determine the stoichiometry of the complex reliably by two-dimensional (2D) classification.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental observations during image processing.

claim: Multivariate statistical analysis indicated unambiguous 13-fold rotational symmetry of the PilQ complex.
source: This procedure indicated unambiguous 13-fold rotational symmetry of the PilQ complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the multivariate statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PilQ complex has a C-terminal secretin domain which inserts into the outer membrane.
source: The complex has a C-terminal secretin domain, which inserts into the OM, and six N-terminal domains that form six stacked rings N0 to N5, which were found to extend deeply into the periplasm (Burkhardt et al., 2011; Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2011 and Gold et al., 2015.

claim: Six N-terminal domains form six stacked rings N0 to N5 that extend deeply into the periplasm.
source: The complex has a C-terminal secretin domain, which inserts into the OM, and six N-terminal domains that form six stacked rings N0 to N5, which were found to extend deeply into the periplasm (Burkhardt et al., 2011; Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2011 and Gold et al., 2015.

claim: Rings N1 to N5 consist of predicted –βαββα– folds.
source: Rings N1 to N5 consist of predicted –βαββα– folds whereas the N0 ring has an unusual –ααβαββα– fold (Burkhardt et al., 2012; Salzer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2012 and Salzer et al., 2016.

claim: The N0 ring has an unusual –ααβαββα– fold.
source: Rings N1 to N5 consist of predicted –βαββα– folds whereas the N0 ring has an unusual –ααβαββα– fold (Burkhardt et al., 2012; Salzer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2012 and Salzer et al., 2016.

claim: The overall PilQ complex is flexible, as shown by 2D class averages.
source: Although the secretin domain resists denaturation even at high temperatures in the presence of SDS (Burkhardt et al., 2011), the 2D class averages show clearly that the overall complex is flexible.
evidence: The claim is supported by the 2D class averages and citation to Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: The cap module shows a distinct rocking movement around an apparent hinge at the interface between rings N4 and N5.
source: The distances between cap and tail and between the rings vary and the cap module shows a distinct rocking movement around an apparent hinge at the interface between rings N4 and N5 (Figure 1I,II,III,IV).
evidence: The claim is supported by the 2D class averages shown in Figure 1.

claim: Initial 3D reconstructions had a resolution of only ~20 Å.
source: Consequently, initial 3D reconstructions had a resolution of only ~20 Å (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the reconstruction shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The structure was split into two modules at the N4 ring and both parts were reconstructed separately by residual signal subtraction (RSS).
source: To improve the map we split the structure into two modules at the N4 ring and reconstructed both parts separately by residual signal subtraction (RSS) (Bai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described and citation to Bai et al., 2015.

claim: 3D classification and auto-refinement improved the resolution of both maps to ~15 Å.
source: 3D classification and auto-refinement improved the resolution of both maps to ~15 Å.
evidence: The claim is supported by the image processing results.

claim: The REcenter Particles (REP) program was written to move the residual signal to any desired position in the box to maximize alignment precision.
source: To improve the map further, we wrote the program REcenter Particles (REP) (Sanchez, 2017) based on the approach of Ilca et al. (2015) and Hou et al., 2017 (see the Appendix for a detailed description of the program). By this procedure the residual signal can be moved to any desired position in the box to maximize alignment precision, and the windows can be cropped to a smaller box size.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the REP program and citations.

claim: The REP procedure was applied to create four new particle data sets for the secretin domain with the N5 ring, the N4 ring, and the N2N3 and N0N1 ring pairs.
source: We applied the REP procedure to create four new particle data sets, one for each of the rigid parts of the PilQ structure, i.e. the secretin domain with the N5 ring, the N4 ring, and the N2N3 and N0N1 ring pairs (Figure 2B–E,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods and Figure 2.

claim: The recentering procedure improved the accuracy of the rotational alignment from ~12° to 2°.
source: This improved the accuracy of the rotational alignment from ~12° to 2°, which doubled the resolution and revealed a wealth of new, interpretable map features (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the alignment statistics.

claim: The final component maps have respective resolutions of 7.6 Å, 6.7 Å, 7.6 Å, 7.0 Å for the secretin-N5 ring, N4 ring, and the N2N3 and N0N1 ring pairs.
source: The final component maps have respective resolutions of 7.6 Å, 6.7 Å, 7.6 Å, 7.0 Å for the secretin-N5 ring, N4 ring, and the N2N3 and N0N1 ring pairs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the resolution statistics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Remote homology detection enabled finding and aligning homologous 3D structures for all PilQ domains.
source: By remote homology detection (see Materials and methods) we were able to find and align homologous 3D structures for all PilQ domains (Table 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling methods and Table 1.

claim: C13 symmetry was imposed on the ring domains and the symmetrized models were fitted to their map regions.
source: C13 symmetry was imposed on the ring domains and the symmetrized models were fitted to their map regions, followed by optimization with a flexible fitting procedure (see Materials and methods; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling methods described.

claim: The C-terminal secretin domain of PilQ was modeled on the basis of the recently determined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of type 2 and type 3 secretion systems.
source: The C-terminal secretin domain of PilQ was modeled on the basis of the recently determined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of type 2 (Yan et al., 2017) and type 3 secretion systems (Worrall et al., 2016) and fills a substantial proportion of the secretin-N5 region.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yan et al., 2017 and Worrall et al., 2016.

claim: The rings of domains N1 to N5 show the conserved -βαββα- motif, typical of the N-terminal part of the secretion systems.
source: The rings of domains N1 to N5 show the conserved -βαββα- motif, typical of the N-terminal part of the secretion systems (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural model shown in Video 1.

claim: Domains N0 and N1 of T. thermophilus PilQ differ from other known N0 and N1 domain structures by long insertions at positions where there are loops in the template structures.
source: Domains N0 and N1 of T. thermophilus PilQ differ from other known N0 and N1 domain structures (Berry et al., 2012; Spreter et al., 2009) by long insertions at positions where there are loops in the template structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with structures from Berry et al., 2012 and Spreter et al., 2009.

claim: The independently reconstructed ring modules matched the corresponding C13 atomic models reasonably well.
source: Overall the independently reconstructed ring modules matched the corresponding C13 atomic models reasonably well, as shown by computation of local cross-correlation (See Materials and methods; Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The PilQ complex is 350 Å long and 125 Å wide.
source: The PilQ complex is 350 Å long and 125 Å wide (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from the structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Thirteen PilQ protomers assemble to form a cylinder with a central channel that connects the outer membrane space with the periplasm.
source: Thirteen PilQ protomers assemble to form a cylinder with a central channel that connects the outer membrane space with the periplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis.

claim: The DDM detergent micelle at the top of the secretin domain identifies the membrane-embedded region of PilQ.
source: The DDM detergent micelle at the top of the secretin domain (Figure 1I–IV) identifies the membrane-embedded region of PilQ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the position of the detergent micelle.

claim: The conserved secretin domain has an outer β-barrel cage consisting of four long β-strands per protomer and two β-hairpins that constitute gate 1.
source: The conserved secretin domain has two distinct features: an outer β-barrel cage consisting of four long β-strands per protomer, and two β-hairpins that constitute gate 1 (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), as observed in the other secretin domains (Koo et al., 2016; Worrall et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis and citations.

claim: Sequence alignment indicated that PilQ lacks the lip domain that forms a cap on the extracellular side of the outer membrane in some species.
source: Sequence alignment to secretins of known 3D structure indicated that PilQ lacks the lip domain that forms a cap on the extracellular side of the OM in some species (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment and citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: The PilQ complex has an additional density outside the outer membrane referred to as the 'crown'.
source: Surprisingly, the PilQ complex has an additional density outside the OM, which we refer to as the 'crown' (Figure 3, Figure 5A, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the cryo-EM map shown in Figures 3 and 5A.

claim: The crown consists of 13 distinct spikes, ~40 Å high, which make contact with the inner surface of the outer β-barrel of the transmembrane part of the secretin.
source: The crown consists of 13 distinct spikes, ~40 Å high, which make contact with the inner surface of the outer β-barrel of the transmembrane part of the secretin.
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis of the crown.

claim: Gate 1 is located immediately below the membrane-embedded portion of the β-barrel and defines a ~30 Å aperture.
source: Gate 1 is located immediately below the membrane-embedded portion of the β-barrel and defines a ~30 Å aperture.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from the structure.

claim: The N5 ring below Gate 1 has an inner diameter of ~70 Å.
source: The N5 ring below Gate 1 has an inner diameter of ~70 Å.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from the structure.

claim: Ring N4 is separated by ~20 Å from the N2N3 pair.
source: Ring N4 is separated by ~20 Å from the N2N3 pair.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from the structure.

claim: The N1 ring harbors Gate 2, which has a 30 Å aperture similar to Gate 1.
source: The N1 ring harbors Gate 2, which has a 30 Å aperture similar to Gate 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from the structure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The crown region of the PilQ complex outside the outer membrane is not accounted for by the PilQ sequence.
source: The crown region of the PilQ complex outside the outer membrane is not accounted for by the PilQ sequence (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the structure with the sequence.

claim: K728 and R730 residues are located just below the detergent belt, close to the TM region of PilQ.
source: Residues R730 and K728 (dark blue) are located just below the detergent belt (grey bar), close to the TM region of PilQ in the modeled homo-oligomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The PilQ K728A/R730A variant forms PilQ complexes lacking the crown region.
source: EM analysis of the PilQ K728A/R730A (PilQ-KR) variant revealed that it forms PilQ complexes lacking the crown region (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM analysis shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: K728 and R730 are not essential for PilQ oligomerization or thermostability.
source: We conclude that K728 and R730 are not essential for PilQ oligomerization or thermostability (Figure 6B), but necessary for crown assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: K728 and R730 are necessary for crown assembly.
source: We conclude that K728 and R730 are not essential for PilQ oligomerization or thermostability (Figure 6B), but necessary for crown assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by the EM analysis of the mutant.

claim: In PilQ-KR particles, the density close to the outer membrane is fuzzy while the remaining complex appears unchanged.
source: In these particles the density close to the OM is fuzzy (Figure 5B), while the remaining complex appears unchanged.
evidence: The claim is supported by the 2D class averages shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The crown module in the PilQ-KR variant has bound but is not properly folded.
source: This observation suggests that the crown module in this PilQ variant has bound but is not properly folded.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the EM observations.

claim: Residues K728 and R730 are important for PilQ crown assembly or folding.
source: These observations illustrate that residues K728 and R730 are important for PilQ crown assembly or folding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The pilQ-KR double mutant showed a twitching zone that was 64% of the wild-type.
source: The pilQ-KR double mutant showed a twitching zone of 1.4 ± 0.3 cm, which was smaller than that of the WT strain (64% of the wild-type).
evidence: The claim is supported by the twitching motility assay data.

claim: The pilQ-KR mutant exhibited only 49% of the wild-type adherence.
source: The pilQ-KR showed a ratio of 1.9 ± 1.3 × 10−2. The pilQ-KR mutant therefore exhibited only 49% of the wild-type adherence.
evidence: The claim is supported by the adherence assay data.

claim: The crown plays a role in type IV pilus-mediated adhesion and twitching motility.
source: These findings suggest that the crown plays a role in type IV pilus-mediated adhesion and twitching motility.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the functional assay data.

claim: The transformability of the pilQ-KR mutant was reduced to 6% of wild-type.
source: The transformability of the pilQ-KR mutant was reduced to 6% (frequency = 1.6 × 10−4± 5.4 × 10−5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the transformation assay data.

claim: K728 and R730 play an essential, functional role in DNA uptake and natural transformation.
source: This suggests that K728 and R730 play an essential, functional role in DNA uptake and natural transformation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the transformation assay data.

claim: The recentering procedure improves the resolution of flexible particles by moving particles from the edge of the box to reduce alignment errors.
source: The overall alignment improved substantially (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), compensating for the small number of available particles. The improvement is easily explained as follows: A small alignment error at the center of the box becomes more severe with increasing distance from the center of rotation. Moving the particles from the edge of the box therefore results in a significant enhancement in the accuracy of local particle alignment.
evidence: The claim is based on logical reasoning about the recentering procedure.

claim: The recentering procedure should be especially useful for large, flexible complexes with multiple components.
source: This feature of our recentering procedure should be especially useful for large, flexible complexes with multiple components such as PilQ and other secretion systems (Worrall et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017), respiratory supercomplexes (Sousa et al., 2016), spliceosomes (Nguyen et al., 2015), apoptosomes (Pang et al., 2015), or stressosomes (Marles-Wright et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the applicability of the method, supported by citations.

claim: The recentering procedure improved the map resolution to ~7 Å, whereas conventional global alignment limits the resolution to ~20 Å.
source: In case of our PilQ complex, this procedure improved the map resolution to ~7 Å, whereas the conventional global alignment procedure limits the resolution to ~20 Å (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the two methods shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: The structure of the T. thermophilus PilQ complex differs from that of other secretion systems.
source: The structure of the T. thermophilus PilQ complex differs from that of other secretion systems (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4.

claim: PilQ is evolutionarily related to other secretins and partly resembles T2SS.
source: PilQ is evolutionarily related to other secretins and partly resembles T2SS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on evolutionary analysis and structural comparison.

claim: Both PilQ and T2SS complexes have an OM-embedded homo-oligomeric secretin domain with a barrel-within-barrel structure.
source: Both complexes have an OM-embedded homo-oligomeric secretin domain with a barrel-within-barrel structure (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Other known secretion systems feature a single gate in the outer membrane (Gate 1), which is a conserved feature amongst all secretins.
source: Other known secretion systems feature a single gate in the OM (Gate 1) (Costa et al., 2015; Korotkov et al., 2011), which is a conserved feature amongst all secretins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2015 and Korotkov et al., 2011.

claim: PilQ from T. thermophilus has an additional gate (Gate 2) on the periplasmic side close to the platform apparatus.
source: PilQ from T. thermophilus has an additional gate (Gate 2) on the periplasmic side close to the platform apparatus, which connects PilQ to a still not yet identified channel in the inner membrane (Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural analysis and citation to Gold et al., 2015.

claim: The unusual number of six N-terminal ring domains makes PilQ one of the largest secretion systems to have been characterized so far.
source: The unusual number of six N-terminal ring domains makes PilQ one of the largest secretion systems to have been characterized so far (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with other secretion systems shown in Figure 4.

claim: The six rings enable the complex to span most of the wide periplasmic space of T. thermophilus.
source: The six rings enable the complex to span most of the wide periplasmic space of T. thermophilus (Burkhardt et al., 2011; Burkhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2011 and 2012.

claim: The N0 ring is well resolved in the map, whereas in other secretins it was not visible, apparently due to its flexibility.
source: The N0 ring is well resolved in the map, whereas in other secretins it was not visible, apparently due to its flexibility (Koo et al., 2016; Worrall et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with other structures and citations.

claim: Multiple sequence alignment of secretin domains reveals a cap/lip segment in some species that forms a protrusion outside the outer membrane.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of secretin domains (Figure 4D) reveals a cap/lip segment in some species that forms a protrusion outside the OM (Koo et al., 2016; Worrall et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4D and citations.

claim: T. thermophilus PilQ does not contain the cap/lip sequence.
source: T. thermophilus PilQ does not contain this sequence; however, our EM map shows a large crown module outside the OM (Video 1, Figure 3), which cannot be assigned to any part of the PilQ sequence (Figure 5A) and thus must be another protein component of the complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and the EM map.

claim: The crown module must be another protein component of the complex.
source: T. thermophilus PilQ does not contain this sequence; however, our EM map shows a large crown module outside the OM (Video 1, Figure 3), which cannot be assigned to any part of the PilQ sequence (Figure 5A) and thus must be another protein component of the complex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The crown module is also visible in sub-tomogram averages of the piliated and the non-piliated complex in situ.
source: The crown module outside the OM is also visible in sub-tomogram averages of the piliated and the non-piliated complex in situ (Gold et al., 2015) (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gold et al., 2015 and Figure 7.

claim: The crown module appears to be difficult to separate from the PilQ secretin domain and resists denaturation with SDS at high temperature.
source: The crown module appears to be difficult to separate from the PilQ secretin domain and resists denaturation with SDS at high temperature (Burkhardt et al., 2011), which indicates a very tight interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Burkhardt et al., 2011.

claim: The tight interaction between the crown and secretin domain indicates a very tight interaction.
source: The crown module appears to be difficult to separate from the PilQ secretin domain and resists denaturation with SDS at high temperature (Burkhardt et al., 2011), which indicates a very tight interaction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the biochemical properties.

claim: PilQ is essential for DNA binding.
source: Our previous finding that PilQ is essential for DNA binding (Schwarzenlander et al., 2009) leads us to conclude that the crown structure is either directly or indirectly implicated in DNA binding and uptake.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schwarzenlander et al., 2009.

claim: The crown structure is either directly or indirectly implicated in DNA binding and uptake.
source: Our previous finding that PilQ is essential for DNA binding (Schwarzenlander et al., 2009) leads us to conclude that the crown structure is either directly or indirectly implicated in DNA binding and uptake.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the functional data.

claim: The crown may be the extracellular switch that converts the pilus extrusion machinery into a DNA uptake system.
source: We speculate that it may be the extracellular switch that converts the pilus extrusion machinery into a DNA uptake system.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the function of the crown.

claim: PilQ forms the core of the bifunctional T4PS/DNA uptake system.
source: PilQ forms the core of the bifunctional T4PS/DNA uptake system and is suggested to interact with a number of periplasmic and outer and inner membrane anchored proteins (Friedrich et al., 2002; Rose et al., 2011; Rumszauer et al., 2006; Salzer et al., 2014; Schwarzenlander et al., 2009; Tsai and Tainer, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The structure provides a firm base for mechanistic investigations of the complex apparatus that enables natural transformation.
source: Our structure provides a firm base for mechanistic investigations of the complex apparatus that enables natural transformation.
evidence: The claim is based on the significance of the structural data.

claim: A total of 932 micrographs was collected for cryo-EM analysis.
source: A total of 932 micrographs was collected.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data collection statistics.

claim: A dataset containing 11,457 particle images was manually picked for image processing.
source: A dataset containing 11,457 particle images manually picked with EMAN boxer (Ludtke et al., 1999) (324 pixels x 324 pixels) was subjected to 2D reference-free classification in RELION (Scheres, 2012) to check the quality of the particle images.
evidence: The claim is supported by the image processing statistics.

claim: The EM maps have been deposited in the EMDB with accession codes EMD-3985 for the full complex and EMD-3995, EMD-3996, EMD-3997 and EMD-3998 for the cap, N4, N2-N3, and N0-N1 domains.
